title: No hot wind touches
hook: no hot wind touches the one in the Lord's refuge (Bilaval M5, ang 819)

segments.voice: Yesterday, holding your hem, and your line: holding the hem. When praise or criticism came, did you let it pass? Today, a shabad many Sikhs sing when someone they love needs protecting. Day six hundred sixty-seven.

In a Punjabi June, the afternoon wind doesn't cool you. It burns. It comes off the plains like the air from an open oven, and people have a name for it: the loo. Shops pull their shutters, farmers rest under the trees, and mothers keep children indoors until evening. Anyone who grew up with that wind knows what shade means. Not a nice extra. Survival. Guru Arjan took that experience and turned it into one of the most-sung lines of comfort in the Granth. Today: no hot wind touches.
screen: `A PUNJABI JUNE AFTERNOON.` → `THE WIND LIKE AN OVEN.` → `WHAT SHADE MEANS.`

segments.voice: The shabad is in Raag Bilaval, on Ang eight nineteen, and it opens: taatee vaao na lagaee, paarbraham sarnaaee. In paraphrase: the hot wind doesn't touch the one who is in the refuge of the Supreme Lord. Then the picture widens. All around me, on four sides, is the Lord's protective circle, so no pain touches me. I met the true Guru, who made this happen; he gave me the medicine of the Lord's Name. Three images hold it together. First, taatee vaao, the hot wind. It stands for whatever scorches: illness, fear, cruelty, grief. Second, sarnaaee, refuge, sanctuary, the place you run to. Third, the circle on four sides, a line drawn around you. It's an old picture of a protected space, a boundary that harm can't cross. Now, what does the shabad promise? It's worth reading carefully. Sikhs who sing it have still been sick, and have still lost people. Sikh teachers usually hear it this way: the hot wind may blow, but it doesn't reach the inside of someone who rests in God. The refuge is real, and it's inward first. That's why families sing it in hospital rooms, before a journey, when a baby is born, or simply at night. It isn't a charm. It's a way of standing in the shade while the loo is blowing, and remembering that the shade is there.
screen: `TAATEE VAAO: THE HOT WIND.` · `SARNAAEE: THE REFUGE.` · `A CIRCLE ON FOUR SIDES.` · `SHADE ON THE INSIDE.` · then, large: `IN HIS REFUGE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find shade and rest. If you can, move to the coolest, quietest spot near you: a shaded window, a chair away from the screen, even just closing your eyes. Sit. Name one hot wind blowing in your life right now. Then picture a circle drawn around you on four sides, and rest inside it for the length of the bell. If you pray, you can say Waheguru, or the shabad's opening words, taatee vaao na lagaee. The bell holds the time.
No hot wind touches. Guru Arjan's line: in the refuge of the Supreme Lord, the scorching wind can't reach you; a protective circle stands on four sides.
Your line: in his refuge. Today, when something scorches, a hard email, bad news, a sharp word, step into the shade for one breath before you answer. Day six hundred sixty-seven.
